subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a range of 0 to 160 for the x parameter and 0 to 120 for the y parameter in the [set sprite position to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Did you tinker with the values in the [pick random] value block to determine the range where the treasure chests will appear?

❓Why do you think it will be helpful to have the treasure sprite’s code in the [on game update every ms] loop instead of the [on start] container block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Randomness can introduce a fun element of surprise into a ninja’s project. Guide the ninja to tinker with x values within the [pick random] bubble to explore its effects.

💡The [on game update every ms] loop creates a repeat loop in the game. This means that the code inside of it will run at a regular interval while the game is played.
steps.instructions:
Begin the treasure hunt by making the treasure chests repeatedly appear on the screen! 


Drag out an [on game update every ms] loop. Then, move all of the code from the [on start] container block into the [on game update every ms] loop. 


Set the treasure sprite’s position randomly by dragging out a [set sprite position to] block and inserting two [pick random] value blocks into its x and y value parameters


Click ▶ to see treasure chests continuously appear in random positions on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the Player sprite's name in the parameter of the [move with buttons] and [set sprite stay in screen] blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Did you select or draw an image that you like for your Player sprite?

❓Did you code your Player in the [on start] container block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [move sprite with buttons] will automatically allow the ninja to move the Player sprite in all directions. They are able to modify this by clicking + and editing the vx and vy values.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the game! 


Create a Player sprite in the [on start] container block, and select or draw an image for the sprite. 


Code the Player sprite to move with the direction buttons on the MakeCode game controller, and prevent it from moving off the screen!


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move around the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Does the [on sprite overlaps sprite] check for an overlap between Player and Goal sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How often do you want the Goal sprite to appear as a treasure-filled chest?

❓ What event needs to be true in order for the [if true then] block to run?



﻿Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [% chance] block determines how likely a certain event will occur. Guide the ninja to tinker with the percent value to determine how often they want a treasure-filled chest to appear on the screen. The higher the number, the more likely the chests will contain treasure.

💡Remind the ninja to replace the sprite name with the otherSprite bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block.

💡Remind the ninja to press CTRL (or Command) on their keyboard to select a single block from the [on game update every ms] loop.
steps.instructions:
Open the treasure chests! Add code to set whether there is treasure inside.


Drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block and set the second sprite kind to Goal. Then, open the Logic code block menu and drag out an [if true then] conditional into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. 


Drag the treasure-filled [set sprite image to] block into the “if” opening in the [if true then] conditional. Replace the sprite name with (otherSprite).


Open the Math code block menu and drag out a [% chance] value block to replace <true> in the [if true then] conditional. Change the number in the white bubble to a percentage value between 0 and 100 to set how likely the chest is to be filled with treasure.

steps.hints: ❓ Is the sprite image in the “else” opening different than the sprite image in the “if” opening?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you click + to add an [else] condition to your [if true then] container block?

❓ How often will an empty treasure chest appear on the screen? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja to notice that the code in the “else” opening will be the remaining percentage of time. In this example, if the treasure-filled chest appears 50% of the time, the empty treasure chest will appear the remaining 50% of time. Encourage the ninja to tinker with this value to determine how often each image will appear on the screen.

💡Remind the ninja to press CTRL (or Command) on their keyboard to select a single block from the [on game update every ms] loop.
steps.instructions:
Add code to display an empty treasure chest!


Click + to add an [else] condition to your conditional. 


Then, drag the empty treasure chest [set sprite image to] block into the “else” opening in the [if true then / else] conditional. Replace the sprite name with (otherSprite).


Click ▶ to see how often the Player sprite finds an empty chest!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [play sound] and destroy the (otherSprite) in both the “if” and “else” openings of the [if true then / else] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Did you test out different effects and sounds and select ones that you like?

❓How did these changes affect the game experience? 

❓What other variables might you add to this game to make it more exciting?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to drag the otherSprite bubble into the [destroy sprite] block, so that the event happens when the Player overlaps with any sprite of a certain kind.
steps.instructions:
Add a score variable to make the Player sprite gain a point when they unlock treasure! 


Add a [set score to] block into the [on start] container block. Add a [change score by] block so that the Player sprite earns a point when they overlap with a treasure-filled chest.


Then add code to play a sound until done and destroy the Goal sprite with a special effect whenever the Player sprite overlaps one.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite overlaps either an “empty” or “full” Goal sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Does your countdown parameter give you enough time to play the game and win, without being too hard or too easy?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What number score should the Player reach to win the game that is high enough so that the game isn’t too easy, but not too high that it’s impossible?

❓ What condition needs to be met in order for the [if true then] block to run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to tinker with the dropdown menu in the [0=0] value block to think about how else they can measure the score to decide whether the game ends in a win or lose.
steps.instructions:
Add a countdown timer to the game! 


Add a [start countdown] block into the [on start] container, and select a time length parameter for this game. 


Drag out an [on countdown end] container block, then place an [if true then] conditional inside. Drag a [game over] block into the “if” opening, and set the toggle to WIN. 


Open the Logic code block menu and drag out a [0=0] value block to replace the <true>. Open the Info code block menu and drag a score value block into the first white bubble of [0=0]. 


In the dropdown menu of [0=0], select the greater than (>) sign, then set the number of points the Player should earn before the countdown ends by typing a number in the second white bubble.


Click ▶ to see if the Player can win the game before the countdown ends!

steps.hints: ❓ In the [on countdown end] container, are there two [game over] blocks used, one in the “if” opening and one in the “else” opening?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓Are the toggles in the [game over] blocks set to the right position?❓How is the [else] condition useful in determining whether the game ends in a win or lose?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡Encourage the ninja to consider how else they might use the [if true then] conditional container block to determine what happens when certain events (i.e. the game ending) occur.
steps.instructions:
Add code to make the Player lose the game if they do not earn enough points before the countdown ends. 


In the [if true then] conditional inside the [on countdown end] container block, click + to add an [else] condition. 


Drag a [game over] block in the “else” opening and set the toggle to LOSE.


Click ▶ to see what happens if the Player does not earn enough points when the timer reaches 0.

steps.hints: 💡 Try adding blocks to customize your game!
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Which block will set a background color? Which block will set screen effects? Which block will set dialog boxes?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?



Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this game by setting a background color, adding a screen effect, and adding directions with dialog boxes!


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a game where the Player has to open as many treasure chests as they can before the time runs out. Collect points only if the treasure chest is full!

validationItems.text: Use a Game Update loop to repeatedly create Goal sprites at random positions.
Add a Player sprite. Code it to move with buttons and stay in screen.
Use an if/else conditional statement with a % chance value block to determine if the Goal sprite is “empty” or “full” when the Player sprite overlaps with it.
Destroy the Goal sprite and change the score if the Goal sprite is “full” when it overlaps with a Player sprite.
Use a countdown timer with an if/else conditional statement to determine what happens when the countdown ends, based on the Player’s score.
Add a background color or image, screen effects, or dialog boxes with game directions

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about conditionals, which are code that makes a decision in a program. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: What if?
badges.description: Use conditionals to make different things happen in a project.

badges.title: To Be or Not to Be?
What are the Chances?
badges.description: Use probability in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Same Difference
badges.description: Compare two values in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Coming from Left Field
badges.description: Launch a projectile from the side of the screen.

badges.title: Weighing the Options
badges.description: Use an if/else statement in a project.
